edits.new: Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus) is the classic heat-loving Southern vegetable, a tall member of the mallow family (Malvaceae, related to cotton and hibiscus, not the nightshades) grown for its tender immature seed pods. It thrives in the hottest part of summer where tomatoes and beans falter, demanding warm soil (at least 65°F at planting, ideally 70°F or more) and a long, hot season to crop well. Plants grow tall, commonly 4 to 6 feet, bear large pale-yellow hibiscus-like flowers, and produce pods that must be picked young (2 to 4 inches) and often (every 1 to 2 days), because they turn woody and inedible within a day or two. Seed is hard-coated and benefits from an overnight soak; many varieties carry spines, so gloves and sleeves help at harvest. Okra is most often direct-sown once soil is warm, about two to three weeks after the last frost, and bears continuously until cold weather. It is well suited to the South, Gulf, and hot interior and desert regions, and marginal in cool-summer areas (the far North and cool coastal California), where it needs transplants, the fastest varieties, and soil-warming tricks, and may still produce only lightly.
